claim: On the abstract indicative Wason task fewer than about 10 percent pick P and not-Q (5 to 30 percent across studies), yet the same logic is solved by a majority under some contents. Abstract form alone is not the whole difficulty; how the rule and goal are read matters.
agent_test: Run 40 abstract conditional-test items vs matched rewrites that state the violation case first, at equal tokens; score exact card set.
audit_note: Cosmides et al. 2010 ('only 5-30%' on indicative rules, 65-80% on social contracts) and Klauer et al. 2007 ('typically fewer than 10%' P and not-Q) support it; the 5-30% range is Cosmides' summary, not a pooled meta-analysis, and Fiddick and Cosmides sources share a lab.

claim: Content helps only for some contents. Early thematic versions failed to replicate; adding realism is not a general fix. What helps is a rule where a violation is clearly defined and worth finding (social contract, precaution, some permission rules).
agent_test: Compare 'add a concrete story' vs 'restate the rule as what counts as a violation' on conditional-test items at equal tokens.
audit_note: Fiddick 2003 (realistic rules failed to replicate Wason and Shapiro; Manktelow and Evans 1979), Cosmides et al. 2010 and Kroger et al. 1993 (permission 47% vs arbitrary 5% only with violation-checking plus explicit negatives) support it; Fiddick and Cosmides are the same theoretical camp, while Kroger/Cheng/Holyoak and Sperber/Girotto are independent rivals.

claim: Social-contract rules with a cheater cue give about 65 to 94 percent correct vs 5 to 45 for matched no-cheater or indicative rules. Cosmides 1989 (Exps 1-9, n=24 or 40 each) gives 71 to 80 (standard) and 65 to 80 (switched) vs 21 to 45; Gigerenzer and Hug (independent lab, n=93) gives 94 vs 44. The '65 to 80' range is Cosmides' own spread, not a cross-lab figure. The additive factors (64, 46, 26, 26 percent for three, two, one, zero) come only from Cosmides 2010.
agent_test: Design hint only: when stating a rule, make explicit who benefits, who could violate it, and whose violation is being checked.
audit_note: Cosmides 2010 (64/46/26 additive factors, 5-30% indicative), Cosmides 1989 pages via 2010 summary, and Gigerenzer and Hug (n=93, 94% vs 44%) match; minor slip: Cosmides' familiar descriptive control was 46%/38%, just above the stated 45% top of the control range; the claim already flags that 65-80 is one lab's spread.

claim: Perspective and the final question steer card choice. Changing 'see whether anyone cheated you' to 'see whether anyone made an exchange with you' dropped P and not-Q from 33-43 percent to 0-10 percent (N=120). Gigerenzer and Hug: employee vs employer cue flips the pattern.
agent_test: Same scenario with two different final questions; check whether the agent's answer follows the stated goal. Equal tokens.
audit_note: Sperber and Girotto 2002 Exp 2 (N=120, 33%/43% vs 10%/0% P and not-Q) and Gigerenzer and Hug 1992 (perspective flips P and not-Q 75% to not-P and Q 61%) match; independent labs; note Sperber and Girotto's cheater cells were below Fiddick et al.'s original (33% vs 66% failed replication).

claim: The cheater-detection result is partly a question-reading effect. With a neutral made-up category (Wason's selection, gliders) P and not-Q reached 91 and 73 percent vs 68 for cheaters (N=100). The need for a dedicated cheater module is contested (Cosmides group replied with precaution and no-if-then data).
agent_test: No agent test; supports not adding a domain-specific cheater module (schema 4b).

claim: Relevance manipulations flip performance in both directions: descriptive rules pushed above 50 percent correct (Prince task 70 vs 25 percent matched control; machine problem 57 percent) and a deontic rule pushed to usual descriptive error when stated no longer in force (15 percent P and not-Q vs 62).
agent_test: Present a deontic rule with a 'no longer in force' context; check that the agent still separates rule status from rule content. Single source because the Sperber group summarises its own work in all lines.

claim: Permission-schema theory: abstract permission rule 61 vs 19 percent over a nondeontic rule (Cheng and Holyoak 1985 Exp 2, second hand). Against it: permission schema predicts equal results across permission rules, contradicted by Cosmides Exp 1 and 2 (80/52/44 percent), and Fiddick's abstract permission (20) and obligation (30) rules did not beat controls (10, 15; n.s.; n=20 per group). Kroger et al. 1993 (UCLA, n=36 to 45 per cell): violation-checking frame plus explicit negatives gives permission 47 vs arbitrary 5 percent; without the negatives 18 vs 8 (n.s.); the same tricks do nothing for arbitrary rules. Cheng and Holyoak 1985 itself still unopened; 61 vs 19 is reported via Cosmides 1989.
agent_test: None; do not build a permission-schema operator.

claim: Adaptive abstract rules (social contract, precaution) beat deontic ones: pooled 48 vs 25 percent (n=20 per group); precaution vs action control h=.93. Small N, one lab that defends the theory.
agent_test: None.

claim: Probabilistic and inference accounts explain much of the abstract-task pattern (information gain model fits 34 meta-analysis studies; inference-guessing model fits 16 of 18 data sets, about 75 percent inference and 25 percent guessing), but the rival model families are not settled (Kellen and Klauer critique; Oberauer failed to replicate probability effects).
agent_test: None direct; do not hard-code a theory of why people fail.

claim: Hints to consider every hidden possibility changed the reasoning parameter but only modestly raised correct selections on the abstract task.
agent_test: Prompt 'for each card list what could be on the other side' vs plain, matched against best-of-n at equal tokens.

claim: Language models show human-like content effects: strong on syllogism belief, clear on Wason (realistic > arbitrary for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5), absent on easy NLI. Item-level model accuracy tracks human accuracy. Belief-inconsistent items hardest (GPT-3.5 31.4 vs 61.1 symbolic).
agent_test: Run our agent on belief-congruent vs incongruent syllogism sets (100 items each); report the gap with and without the scaffold at equal tokens.
audit_note: Lampinen et al. (Wason z>2.2, NLI no effect with ceiling, item-level t(832)=3.49, t(345)=4.98) and Ando et al. NeuBAROCO (GPT-3.5 31.37% inconsistent vs 61.05% symbolic) match; the NLI null is partly due to ceiling effects, and the claim omits that stronger models show little belief effect (see K12).

claim: Few-shot examples do not remove content effects (Chinchilla 5-shot: Wason effect grew; ICL often cut accuracy). Zero-shot chain of thought strongly cuts bias in strong open models (Qwen2.5-32B CE 0.348 to 0.096; Qwen3-14B 0.213 to 0.014), yet weaker LLaMA models still lose on unbelievable valid syllogisms (70.74 to 52.59; 32.22 to 19.26).
agent_test: Compare direct, CoT and scaffold on incongruent syllogisms; CE = acc(congruent) - acc(incongruent), equal tokens.
audit_note: Lampinen et al. (Chinchilla 5-shot Wason content effects exaggerated), Bertolazzi et al. 2025 (CE 0.348 to 0.096; 0.213 to 0.014 with CoT) and Bertolazzi et al. 2024 (LLaMA-3 8B 70.74 to 52.59, LLaMA-2-inst 7B 32.22 to 19.26) match; 'ICL often cut accuracy' rests on other sources I did not open.

claim: Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded and aligned inside open models (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls); a debias vector cut CE from 0.348 to 0.072 and conditional activation steering (K-CAST) gave up to 15 points absolute on models that static steering could not fix. Chain-of-thought prompting alone also cut CE substantially in strong open models (0.348 to 0.096), so text prompting reaches part of the effect, while steering offers a further internal lever.
agent_test: None for a prompt-only agent. a27 and b15 are one paper; the two independent sources are Bertolazzi et al. and Valentino et al.
audit_note: Cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, debias vector CE 0.348 to 0.072, and K-CAST up to 15% absolute match, but 'not reachable by a text scaffold' is contradicted by the same Bertolazzi et al. paper, where chain-of-thought alone cut CE 0.348 to 0.096 and 0.213 to 0.014; also the two Bertolazzi entries are versions of one paper.
claim_before_audit: Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded and aligned inside models (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls); a debias vector cut CE 0.348 to 0.072; conditional activation steering gave up to 15 points on small Llama. Not reachable by a text scaffold.

claim: Modern LLMs show the deontic advantage on Wason: deontic beat descriptive for every model and prompt by +5 to +45 points (paper text says 5.0 to 41.2; its Table 2 shows +45 for qwen3-14b zero-shot). Reasoning models reach 97.5 to 100 percent on deontic; errors fit matching bias. 80 problems per cell, exact-match multi-select.
agent_test: Pair each descriptive conditional with a deontic rewrite; test whether rewriting the rule as an obligation before choosing tests lifts accuracy.

claim: Slow human responders show the realistic-content advantage; fast ones do not. Longer time predicts accuracy (z=4.44). A performance bonus changed nothing. Suggests deliberation, not motivation, restores logic. Budget lever in LLMs: the only within-model contrasts found are BIS Reasoning (GPT-5-nano 69.2 percent at minimum effort vs 98.8 at medium; Qwen3-32B 99.58 without vs 99.12 with thinking) and they are two-level, belief-inconsistent items only, so no gap can be computed. Qwen3-Next Thinking still shows a +28 point belief gap (Poddar). In humans, complexity matters: belief wins over logic mainly on the most complex syllogisms (Trippas 2017). No budget sweep on one mid-size model exists (searched; none found).
agent_test: Vary thinking-token budget on matched congruent and incongruent items for a mid-size model and a frontier model; check whether the belief gap shrinks at fixed total tokens. Scale checking with item complexity.

claim: Models are brittle to surface content beyond logic tasks: changing numerical values lowers GSM accuracy (changing names alone mainly adds variance), adding one irrelevant but plausible clause drops accuracy by up to 65 percent (GSM-NoOp), and on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks performance degrades substantially and consistently relative to the default versions (Wu et al.).
agent_test: Abstraction operator (restate with placeholders, solve, map back) vs direct on perturbed items, equal tokens; measure variance across renamings.
audit_note: GSM-Symbolic found accuracy falls when numbers (or names plus numbers) change, but changing names alone leaves GSM8K performance near the name-changed distribution (only extra variance); the 65% figure is a maximum and Wu et al. report 'substantial and consistent' degradation over 11 tasks (not verified per task).
claim_before_audit: Models are brittle to surface content beyond logic tasks: changing names and numbers lowers GSM accuracy, one irrelevant clause drops it up to 65 percent; counterfactual rule versions fall below default on all 11 tasks.

claim: Higher cognitive ability goes with better abstract selection performance but not with deontic problems; about 10 percent of students use System 2 on the task. Seen in abstract and secondary citation only; a later review says ability predicted deontic tasks less well but mostly in the same direction, so the abstract's 'unrelated' wording is not safe to quote. Full text of Stanovich and West (1998) could not be obtained in the gap pass (ResearchGate and repository links blocked; only a book review came back).
agent_test: None until the primary paper is read.

claim: Abstraction (separating form from content) has real but size-dependent evidence. For weak or mid models, extract-the-form pipelines cut belief bias a lot: SemEval-2026 Task 11 set-notation pipeline 98.95 percent accuracy and CE 2.13 vs 71.70 for a Gemma3-7B direct baseline (but no strong-model direct arm); Qwen3 4B Thinking 95.83 with FOL plus prover vs 84.17 direct. For a strong model the headroom is small: Gemini 3 Flash asked directly 98.43 (CE 2.13) vs 100 (CE 0.0) after normalise-and-parse. Zero-shot CoT leaves a big residual on 7B to 14B models (BPA 72.0 average vs 97.0 for activation steering, which needs weights). Prompt-only QuaSAR gives small gains on GPT-4o-class models (GSM8K 94.5 to 96.5) and hurts small ones; Step-Back's gain over CoT is +1.6 / +0.3 for GPT-4 on MMLU Physics / Chemistry. No source compares abstraction to plain CoT at equal tokens on current models.
agent_test: Form-extraction step vs plain CoT vs plain direct, on matched congruent/incongruent syllogisms and Wason items, at equal total tokens, 3 seeds, one weak, one mid, one frontier model; report the gap by model.

claim: Making the logical relation of a rule explicit before reasoning raises correct selection in humans. Ahn and Graham 1999 (n=22): with necessity-sufficiency spelled out, 50 percent of responses on abstract letter-number rules were normative vs 18 percent P and not-Q in the control. Macchi 2019 (n=130): 'necessarily follow' wording lifts invalid-believable syllogisms from 4-10 to 66-77 percent. Kroger 1993: violation-checking frame plus explicit negatives lifts permission rules to 47 percent vs 5 for arbitrary.
agent_test: Add a 'restate: what counts as a violation, what is needed vs enough, whose violation' step; compare to plain CoT at equal tokens on Wason-like and incongruent-syllogism items.
audit_note: Ahn and Graham (n=22; control P and not-Q .18), Macchi et al. (control 4%/10%; Necessarily 66%/77%) and Kroger et al. (47% vs 5%) match; minor slip: n=130 is Macchi's Exp 1 control sample, the 'necessarily' groups are smaller (N=82 combined), and Ahn and Graham's 50% is a mean over three explicated conditions rather than the same measure as the control's 18% P and not-Q.

claim: On current LLMs a short task-restating instruction recovers most belief-bias errors: of 100 syllogisms GPT-4o got wrong, 'focus strictly on logic, follows necessarily' (which also names the belief inconsistency) recovered 76 percent, CoT 87, plain prompt 5. Errors-only sample, prompts of different length, no equal-token comparison. Human data support goal framing: the same descriptive rule gave 16.7 percent P and not-Q under a truth-seeking question and 50.0 when the goal was to find people at risk (Fiddick et al. 2000, n=30 per cell), while telling people to judge only logic left a conflict cost of .17 to .24 in accuracy on logic judgments (Trippas 2017). So the framing helps when it names what counts as a violation, not when it just says 'be logical'.
agent_test: Run restate-the-violation vs CoT vs plain at equal tokens on all items (not only failures); add a 'be logical' control without the violation wording.

claim: Belief bias on syllogisms is small or absent in current top models but large in mid-size ones, and not tied to the thinking label or to size. Poddar (14 models): Gemini 2.5 Pro +1.4, Flash +0.9, GPT-OSS-20B +0.8, Llama 3.3 70B +31.6, Qwen3-Next Thinking +28.0; mean +10.8. BIS: GPT-5-mini 99.7, GPT-4o 79.5. SemEval overview baselines: Qwen3 14B 97.38 acc with content effect 4.23, but Qwen2.5 14B 67.50 with 44.54 and Phi-4 15B 83.33 with 14.89. A strong model asked directly sits at 98.43 (CE 2.13), so the room for a debias step on frontier models is about two points.
agent_test: Do not add a belief-debias step by default for frontier models; measure the gap on a small congruent/incongruent probe and add the step only if the gap is above a set threshold.

claim: The LLM deontic advantage on Wason (+5 to +45) cannot yet be separated from the 'must' wording or from topic familiarity. Abe et al. defines deontic rules by obligation or prohibition words and descriptive rules as arbitrary if-then rules with no modal word, so content, modal word and format all change together (160 problems, 80 per type, 20 per polarity). The nearest content-by-rule-type control for LLMs (Seals and Shalin 2024, 7B-class models, n=70 social and 70 non-social problems) found a smaller social-rule advantage than in humans and did not vary the modal word. In humans, the content effect survived with no if-then rule and no modal (66.7 percent P and not-Q with a rule vs 50.0 with only stated wants, n=30 each), and schema theory itself treats 'must' vs 'may' as part of the mechanism. A paired 2x2 (and a question-only cell) has not been run.
agent_test: 2x2: norm vs arbitrary content x 'must' vs plain 'is' wording on the same four-card logic, plus a cell that changes only the final question (look for violations vs test the rule), plus a switched-contract item.

claim: Relevance manipulations have large primary effects (Sperber 1995): 78 vs 26 percent (n=27 within), 65 vs 16 (n=17/19), 70 vs 25 (n=20 per cell), and with effect x effort 57, 38, 38, 5 percent (n=21 per cell). A cross-check from another lab design: changing only the question from truth-seeking to precaution moved P and not-Q from 16.7 to 50.0 percent (Fiddick et al. 2000, n=30 per cell). Transfer to LLMs is untested: three targeted searches found no study that manipulates relevance-theory predictions in prompts. Ragni et al. 2018 (Table 4 effect sizes) is paywalled; no open copy was found.
agent_test: Ask for the card or case that would falsify the rule, and name the not-Q case, vs plain; compare at equal tokens.

claim: A violation-framing instruction is not universal: Valina et al. found it helped a thematic permission rule but not the obligation or abstract versions (instruction x content interaction); Platt and Griggs' ~80 percent abstract result (second hand) needed an explained rule and a request for reasons, and the schema authors dispute how Platt and Griggs (1993) read their cost-benefit result. Fiddick et al. (2000) cite violation instructions alone as failing for abstract and descriptive rules in several older studies, with Platt and Griggs 1993 Exp 3 as an exception (second hand). No source tests sorting a rule as descriptive or prescriptive first, in humans or in models.
agent_test: Make the violation step conditional on rule type; test the sort-first step as its own arm.

claim: Surface content changes accuracy of LLMs even when logic is fixed: counterfactual worlds lower GPT-4 (FOLIO 93.8 default vs 74.1 counterfactual, no CoT; 81 items), symbols vs semantics shift deduction (Symbolic Tree ChatGPT 71.8 vs 53.7), and irrelevant clauses or name/number swaps cut GSM accuracy (up to 65 percent drop, Phi-3-mini). Several independent labs agree on direction.
agent_test: Run the same items with names, nouns and counterfactual framing swapped; compare plain vs a form-extraction step at equal tokens.
audit_note: FOLIO 93.8 vs 74.1 (81 items), Symbolic Tree ChatGPT 71.8 vs 53.7, and Phi-3-mini over 65% NoOp drop all match; slip: the 65% drop is for the irrelevant clause (NoOp), not for name or number swaps, and name-only swaps do not clearly lower accuracy.

claim: Abstraction prompts (Step-Back, Take a Step Back; QuaSAR) improve STEM and multi-hop tasks over the plain prompt (PaLM-2L Physics 66.4 to 73.2, Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA +27; GPT-4 Physics 69.4 to 84.5). Over zero-shot CoT the gain is smaller: PaLM-2L +8.2 Physics and +6.5 Chemistry, GPT-4 +1.6 and +0.3 (sd about 0.5 to 1.5), and Step-Back was 0.9 below CoT on StrategyQA for PaLM-2L. Old models, no equal-token arm, no belief-bias or Wason test.
agent_test: Step-back question vs CoT at matched total tokens on a mixed set of reasoning items; check gain shrinks on a current model.

claim: Offloading logical form to a solver helps most where depth is high (Logic-LM minus CoT on ProofWriter GPT-4: +7.1 at depth 0 to +39.4 at depth 5; SatLM GSM-SYS 69.4 greedy) and for small models (Qwen3 4B Thinking: FOL plus prover 95.83 vs 84.17 direct), but not always: LINC with GPT-4 on FOLIO 72.5 vs CoT 75.3. On syllogisms, pure Z3 gave 97.6 on invalid but 52.2 on valid items (CE 26.28) because the LLM form-extraction step fails on valid items. The best hybrid on belief-inconsistent items found is a Z3 tiebreaker on 3-2 ensemble splits: 94.3 vs 93.4 percent, CE 2.85 vs 3.39, net +8 of 960 items, inside one sd, at about 4,300 tokens per item. A strong model asked directly scores 98.43 (CE 2.13).
agent_test: Add a formalise-and-check operator used only when two independent passes disagree; never as a veto; score by depth and by belief-consistent vs inconsistent items; count tokens against a single strong pass with more thinking.

claim: Order and premise arrangement, not only content, move LLM accuracy: shuffling premises drops deductive accuracy by 20 to 30 points for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L and over 40 points (from over 65 to below 25 percent) for Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo; reordered GSM8K statements cost GPT-4-turbo 94.1 to 85.0, PaLM 2-L 86.4 to 79.5, Gemini 1.0 Pro 80.5 to 69.1. Best order is the proof order, which is unknown at test time. No paper tests a reorder step; that stays untested.
agent_test: Shuffle premise order on logic items; test a reorder-to-dependency-order step at equal tokens.

claim: A solver as final authority is harmful on syllogisms; a solver as tiebreaker is a small gain. Z3 veto gave 74.1 percent accuracy (CE 26.70) vs 93.4 for the plain ensemble, because form extraction by an LLM breaks on valid items; the tiebreaker on 7.9 percent of items (3-2 splits) added 0.9 points with 19 correct and 11 wrong overrides. Cost about 6 model calls and 4,300 tokens per item.
schema_part: O# (formalise and check) as a tie-break only
agent_test: Compare tie-break-by-second-pass vs tie-break-by-solver vs more thinking at equal tokens on belief-inconsistent items.

claim: On current strong models the room for a form-extraction or solver step on plain syllogisms is about two points. Gemini 3 Flash asked directly: 98.43 accuracy, CE 2.13 (n=192); with normalise-and-parse: 100, CE 0.0. The big gains in the shared task come from weaker baselines (Gemma3-7B 71.70, Qwen2.5 7B 74.31 / CE 31.20, Qwen3 4B Thinking 84.17 direct).
agent_test: Gate the extra step on a measured gap, not on a fixed rule.

claim: In humans the content effect does not need the word 'must' or an if-then statement, but it does need a goal that makes a violation salient. Trade problem with stated wants only (no rule): 50.0 percent P and not-Q vs 66.7 with a stated rule (n=30 each). Same descriptive rule, question changed from truth-seeking to precaution: 16.7 vs 50.0 percent (n=30 each). Both from one lab that defends the social-contract view; schema theory by contrast treats 'must' as part of its mechanism.
agent_test: Question-only arm in the A01.03-K22 2x2.

claim: In humans, 'judge only the logic' instructions do not remove the belief cost, and belief gains ground as problems become more complex. Modus ponens/tollens with a logic instruction: .73 and .69 accuracy on conflict items vs .97 and .86 without conflict (Trippas 2017, Exp 1, about 43 analysed); conflict .68 vs .92 overall. For the most complex three-term multiple-model syllogisms belief interfered with validity judgments more than the reverse.
agent_test: Check whether a 'be logical' control arm underperforms a violation-naming arm in the equal-token test.

claim: Zero-shot CoT removes part but not all of the belief cost in small and mid-size open models, and gains differ a lot by model. Bias-penalised accuracy, baseline to CoT: Qwen-2.5-7B 50.8 to 81.7; Gemma-2-9B 51.8 to 69.9; Mistral-7B 30.2 to 34.3; average 58.1 to 72.0 (vs 97.0 with weight-level steering). Fold-0 subset for some CoT runs.
agent_test: Report CoT residual gap per model, not a pooled average.

claim: Answer format and the question asked change model accuracy on syllogisms. Models almost never answer 'nothing follows' when asked what follows (accuracy near 0 percent for PaLM 2 with zero-shot CoT, 30 samples per item); a binary 'does this conclusion follow?' format raises accuracy on those items a lot. Pretrained LLaMA and Pythia models also almost never say 'nothing follows'. Even the best PaLM 2 reaches only about 75 percent vs about 50 for people, with order-of-terms and fallacy errors that remain when content is neutral.
schema_part: S3/S4 (ask as a binary check; score all candidate conclusions in code)
agent_test: Same syllogisms asked as 'what follows?' vs 'does conclusion X follow?' for each candidate X, scored in code, at equal tokens; report accuracy on 'nothing follows' items.
audit_note: Eisape et al. (about 75% vs about 50%, near 0% on 'nothing follows', 30 samples at temp 0.5, binary discrimination markedly higher on those items) and Bertolazzi et al. (pretrained LLaMA/Pythia rarely say 'nothing follows') match; the 'does this conclusion follow' wording is the notes' description of Eisape's binary-validity method.

claim: A human-like benefit from realistic or social content is not reliable in LLMs outside the Lampinen setup. Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi: the facilitated (post-office) Wason did not help seven models the way it helps people; answers were inconsistent over ten runs and often illogical in non-human ways (GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning in 69.2 percent of all task cases, Claude 2 55.0, Llama 2 7B wrong in 77.5). Seals and Shalin: 7B-class models solve social-rule problems about 30 percent vs about 70 for people, with an odd format interaction. Lampinen: realistic rules do beat arbitrary ones for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (z>2.2). Abe: deontic beats descriptive in nine open models (+5 to +45). Directions agree in some studies and not in others; models, scoring and stimuli differ.
schema_part: G (do not assume human-like help from content)
agent_test: Measure our own agent on a matched realistic / arbitrary / nonsense Wason set with free-text output, 10 runs per item, and report consistency as well as accuracy.

claim: Models use stored world knowledge as a shortcut, and it helps or hurts depending on whether it agrees with the stated premises. Counterfactual rule versions lower accuracy on all 11 task families (GPT-4 two-digit addition base 10 100.0 vs base 9 23.4); false-premise FOLIO items: GPT-4 93.8 vs 74.1 (81 items). Symbolic Tree deduction: removing the in-context rules and facts barely changed ChatGPT (70.1 vs 71.8), so it was using memory. PrOntoQA: with a true ontology the model can skip hops and does not lose accuracy from 3 to 5 hops. On belief-inconsistent data the small syllogism circuit fails and extra attention heads inject world knowledge.
schema_part: G3 (test on a relabelled or counterfactual copy) / S1 input hygiene
agent_test: For each logic item, also run a renamed or counterfactual copy; flag any answer that changes. Report the flip rate per arm at equal tokens.
audit_note: Wu et al. (93.8 vs 74.1 on 81 FOLIO items; consistent drops on 11 tasks), Tang et al. (70.1 vs 71.8), and Saparov and He (true ontology allows skipping hops) match; Kim et al. only report 'evidence of partial contamination' from extra attention heads, so 'inject world knowledge' is stated more firmly than the paper; 'so it was using memory' is Tang's inference.

claim: The step that turns text into logic has its own failure direction, so formalisation helps less than the solver's accuracy suggests. GPT-4 translated syllogisms into predicate logic correctly 96.67 percent of the time (87 of 90) yet final accuracy rose only from 77.78 to 83.33; GPT-3.5 gained nothing (58.89 to 52.22 / 54.44). Z3 fed LLM-extracted formulas scored 74.7 percent (invalid 97.6, valid 52.2). LINC FOL syntax-error rates were 38 percent (StarCoder+), 24 (GPT-3.5), 13 (GPT-4). In contrast a 4B model translated well but reasoned badly, so a prover gave +11.7 points. The weak link depends on model size and data, not on one fixed step.
schema_part: O formalise-and-check (tie-break only; fallback to plain answer)
agent_test: Check the translation on a held-out paraphrase; treat 'solver says not entailed' as weak evidence; compare to a single strong pass at equal tokens.
audit_note: Ozeki et al. (87/90 = 96.67%, 77.78 to 83.33; GPT-3.5 58.89 to 52.22/54.44), FregeLogic (Z3 74.7%, invalid 97.6, valid 52.2), LINC (syntax errors 38/24/13%) and Kartac et al. (95.83 vs 84.17, +11.7) all match; the closing 'weak link depends on size and data' is the notes' synthesis, and the Z3 figure comes from one SemEval system paper.

claim: Inside open models there are two routes: a form route that works on abstract syllogisms and a content route that can override it. A small circuit suppresses the middle term on symbolic syllogisms across sizes; on belief-inconsistent data it fails to recover, and extra heads inject world knowledge (Kim et al.). Validity and plausibility are aligned directions (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls), and more alignment means a larger content effect (Bertolazzi et al.). Conditional steering gives up to 15 points (Valentino et al.). All need weights.
schema_part: none (not reachable by text; supports keeping content out of the input)
agent_test: None for an API-only agent. Use only as the reason to test content-stripped input.
audit_note: Kim et al. (recovery fails on belief-inconsistent data, 'suggesting' extra heads), Bertolazzi et al. (cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, alignment tracks content effect) and Valentino et al. (up to 15% absolute with K-CAST) match; hedged wording in Kim is firmer in the claim, Kim and Valentino share authors (Valentino, Freitas), and the claim is a three-paper synthesis with each finding resting on one paper.

claim: Stripping content to symbols is not a safe fix for a pure LLM. ChatGPT / GPT-4 on Symbolic Tree deduction: semantics 71.8 / 90.0 vs symbols 53.7 / 67.6 vs counter-commonsense 48.9 / 73.4; induction symbols as low as 7.14 for ChatGPT. GPT-3.5 on NeuBAROCO scored 61.05 on symbol items vs 56.89 on consistent and 31.37 on inconsistent. But on syllogisms top models are nearly lossless under nonsense renaming (Gemini 2.5 Flash consistency 99.2 percent natural vs nonsense). Symbols pay only when a program or a strong model does the reasoning on the stripped form.
schema_part: O abstract / S1 (gate by model strength)
agent_test: Natural vs nonsense-renamed copy of the same items at equal tokens for a weak, a mid and a frontier model; report accuracy and flip rate.

claim: Step-by-step reasoning and extra examples are not a safe default when content conflicts with the rules. Zero-shot CoT lowered PaLM-2 base-10 and base-16 addition and chord-playing; on ProofWriter with odd semantics CoT was worse than zero-shot (ChatGPT, pattern only); few-shot CoT raised Llama 4 Maverick's content effect from 3.83 to 10.11 in the SemEval ensemble (simple CoT had the lowest average CE, 5.24); few-shot lowered mean accuracy (79.1 vs 82.7 zero-shot) across 14 models; up to 16 CoT demos do not close the counterfactual gap. Against this, zero-shot CoT cuts content effect strongly in strong open models (A01.03-K12).
schema_part: G1/G11 (extra reasoning only on a signal)
agent_test: Direct vs short CoT vs few-shot CoT on congruent and incongruent items per model; report the gap and the easy-item loss.
audit_note: Minor: the Maverick 3.83 to 10.11 and simple-CoT 5.24 figures come from the Phase 1 prompt comparison on a 200-sample inner subset (5.24 averaged over 3 models), not from the final SemEval ensemble; Tang numbers are only a pattern.

claim: Scoring method, answer format and run-to-run noise can swamp the content effect in measurements, so absolute numbers in this field are fragile. Lampinen: raw-likelihood scoring with an instruction prompt made several models answer 'valid' to everything on syllogisms, and on Wason, scoring without the prior correction gave PaLM 2-L over 75 percent in every condition (including arbitrary and nonsense) although Chinchilla got worse. Eisape: generative vs binary format changed 'nothing follows' accuracy from near 0 to 'markedly higher'. Macmillan-Scott: ten runs per prompt gave highly inconsistent answers. Poddar used adaptive majority voting. The direction of the content effect is broadly stable across scoring choices; the size is not.
schema_part: harness (fix scoring, format, seeds before comparing arms; G7)
agent_test: Fix a single answer format and scoring code for all arms; run at least 3 seeds; report spread with every gap.
audit_note: Lampinen Appx B.2 says PaLM 2-L scored over 75% in every Wason condition WITHOUT the prior correction (raw likelihood), not with prior-corrected scoring as the claim says; the other parts check out.
